name: Actinic Keratosis
description: Actinic keratosis is a rough, scaly patch on the skin caused by years of sun exposure. It is considered a pre-cancerous lesion because some patches may turn into squamous cell skin cancer if left untreated.
common_symptoms: A rough, dry, or sandpaper-like patch of skin
Flat to slightly raised scaly crust
Pink, red, tan, or skin-colored patch
Itching, burning, or tender sensation when touched
Commonly found on the face, scalp, ears, neck, hands, or forearms
causes: Cumulative damage to skin cells from chronic ultraviolet (UV) light exposure from sunlight or tanning booths
risk_factors: Fair skin that burns or freckles easily in the sun
Extensive outdoor work or recreational sun exposure
Bald scalp exposed to direct sunlight
first_aid: Do not scratch, pick, or peel the rough scabs
Gently moisturize the area with fragrance-free lotion
Wear a hat and sunscreen to protect the spot from more sun
Consult a dermatologist or health clinic for evaluation
precautions: Use broad-spectrum sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher every morning
Wear wide-brimmed hats to shade your face, ears, and neck
Stay out of midday sun between 10 AM and 4 PM
Check your skin regularly for changing or hardening spots
home_care: Gently wash the area with mild soap and water
Keep skin hydrated with plain petroleum jelly or gentle moisturizer
Never attempt chemical peels or acid treatments at home
do_not: DO NOT scratch or pick off the rough crusts, as they will return and may bleed
DO NOT use unprescribed wart removers or caustic creams
DO NOT ignore patches that become thicker, tender, or start bleeding
red_flags: The patch rapidly grows thicker, harder, or raises up into a horn-like bump
The area becomes painful, red, swollen, or starts bleeding spontaneously
The spot does not heal after several weeks
when_to_see_doctor: See a doctor or dermatologist promptly if you notice persistent rough or scaly patches on sun-exposed skin, especially if they become thick, painful, or bleed.
prevention: Apply broad-spectrum sunscreen daily to all exposed skin
Wear protective clothing, broad hats, and UV-blocking sunglasses
Avoid tanning beds and artificial UV lamps
